stages.title: Aggregate supply and national income
stages.sub: How the AS curve is built, how it meets AD to fix output and prices, and how shifts change both.

steps.q: Across the whole economy, firms decide how much total output to produce and sell at each possible price level. What is this total amount firms plan to sell at each price level called?
steps.right: The total output firms plan to supply at each price level
steps.wrong: The total output households plan to buy at each price level
steps.hint: Think about who is doing the producing and selling here, not the buying.

steps.q: You want to show, on a diagram with the price level on one axis and real output on the other, how much firms supply at every possible price level. What do you need to do with that information?
steps.right: Plot it as a curve linking price level to output supplied
steps.wrong: Plot it as a single point at the current price
steps.hint: A single point only shows one price. You need the whole relationship shown.

steps.q: On the same diagram you already know how to draw the AD curve sloping down, and now the AS curve sloping up. At the output level where they cross, is there any reason for total output to move away from that point?
steps.right: No, that output level can be sustained
steps.wrong: Yes, output keeps changing after that point
steps.hint: Away from the crossing point, either buyers or sellers would want a different amount than the other side offers. At the crossing point, do they match?

steps.q: A rise in investment (an injection) increases total spending, so the AD curve shifts to the right. Looking at where the new AD curve crosses the unchanged AS curve, compared with the old crossing point, what happens to both the price level and real output?
steps.right: Both the price level and real output rise
steps.wrong: Only real output rises, the price level stays the same
steps.hint: Look at the new crossing point on the diagram: has it moved up as well as across?
